1:
Whether these verses belong to the preceding chapter is the first thing settled. Gill reports that the Hebrew Bible and the Greek and Latin versions attach them to what came before, as though the proclamation celebrated the deliverance from the furnace, and rejects it: they preface a dream and an event concerning the king himself, and rightly begin a new chapter, as the Syriac and Arabic have them. Calvin reaches the same conclusion from the shape of the writing: the edict is set out in the king's name, and other events are inserted, so that the prophet speaks first in the king's person, then narrates in his own, then returns. He grants the transitions are rough, but since they leave the sense neither doubtful nor obscure there is no reason to be troubled by them. He adds his account of why the chapter exists: the king had been sufficiently instructed in the worship of Israel's God and compelled to confess him, yet never left his own superstitions, so his conceptions of the true God were momentary and what follows is the wages of that ingratitude.

The opening title is read as evidence of a changed man. Gill notes that the edict begins with no pompous style but only Nebuchadnezzar the king, since he was now humbled under the mighty hand of God; whether the conversion was real he will not say is evident, though the king speaks of the divine sovereignty in stronger terms than ever before. Henry makes the same observation and dates it: if the king had once used great swelling words in his titles he now lays them aside, being old, lately recovered from a distraction that had mortified him, and at that moment contemplating God's greatness. Wesley goes further than either, holding that nothing less than a real change of heart could produce such a confession from a man of forty years' reign who had seen as much of the world as most men ever do.

The document itself interests the historians. Clarke calls it a regular decree and one of the most ancient on record, and summarises the whole chapter as a state paper in which the king acknowledges the hand of God in his late malady. Ellicott places it in the blank of eighteen years that falls over the end of the reign, whose only known facts are the mania that kept the king under restraint and the later extension of his dominions; from the address to all the earth he infers that time had passed since the previous chapter, the king having grown powerful enough to think himself universal monarch. He adds a suspicion about the authorship, that the scriptural phrases scattered through the letter suggest Daniel wrote it at the king's request. Wesley supposes it was put into the archives and court rolls; Henry that the king published his own infamy because nobody else would have dared, which is why the original paper survives.

The greeting and the doxology are handled briefly and warmly. Ellicott and Wesley both identify the salutation as the ordinary eastern form, and Henry turns it into a maxim, that it becomes kings to disperse their good wishes with their commands and, as fathers of their country, to bless their subjects. On the exclamation that follows, Gill piles up superlatives: the signs are so great it cannot be conceived how great, and so mighty that no power of nature or hell can resist them, and if this holds of providence how much more of grace. Clarke reads the same words as evidence of a mind deeply impressed with the majesty of God, and calls the sentiments very fine. Keil and Delitzsch keep to structure, setting the chapter out as a proclamation in which the living God of heaven made himself known as ruler over the kingdoms of men.
4:
The date of the dream is fixed by arithmetic. Gill works back from the reign: forty-five years in all, the dream fulfilled a year after it came, seven years in the fulfilling and a year or two of life after the restoration, which puts it near the thirty-fifth year; and he cites the chronologers who set it in one year or the next. Henry reaches almost the same point and adds the occasion, that the king had lately finished his wars by conquering Egypt and made himself monarch of those parts; and he explains why the warning was given at all, that when the thing came to pass the king might compare it with the prediction, see that it was the Lord's doing, and learn that there is a divine revelation in the world as well as a divine providence, the works of God agreeing with his word. Clarke names the conquests and draws the moral straight from them, that it was probably these that puffed him up and brought the chastisement on. Ellicott notes only that the Greek version dates this chapter, like the last, to the eighteenth year.

The word for the king's flourishing is heard as a plant word. Ellicott says it is generally used of the growth of trees, and takes it to have been chosen because of the dream that follows. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point and add the abruptness with which the dream is introduced, which they think illustrates the suddenness of the thing itself; they gloss the word for quiet as undisturbed and secure prosperity. Wesley puts it plainly, that with the wars over he sat down quiet and enjoyed the spoils of his enemies. Gill draws the pastoral conclusion, that God can make the minds of the greatest men uneasy in the middle of all their glory and pleasure, since the king did not understand what he had seen and only knew it boded ill.

The failure of the wise men is treated as the point of the delay. Calvin is contemptuous of the whole class: they covered their shamelessness with honourable titles, called themselves learned when they knew no art or science, and deluded men with miserable predictions. He draws the inference the narrative wants: either the science was a fallacy altogether, or at least the interpretation that follows came not by human skill but by revelation, which is what the king meant to say. Gill supplies a providential reason for Daniel coming last, whether sent for or not, that the magicians might first be seen to be baffled, and that Daniel, or rather Daniel's God, might be the more glorified. Ellicott offers an administrative reason instead, that as chief of the governors of the wise men he would not come in until last.

The names given to Daniel are read for what they concede and what they cost. Ellicott points out that the spirit of the holy gods means the king's own gods, since although he had recognised a high God he acknowledged him only as one among many. Gill weighs why the man is called master of the magicians, either because he excelled them, though he would have scorned to be counted of their order, or because the king had set him over them and over their governors. Calvin makes the address a humiliation on both sides: the king, who had not sought Daniel first but consulted his magicians, is now compelled to venerate the man he had passed over; and the Babylonian name he uses would have wounded the prophet deeply, since his own name marked him a Jew of a holy and elect nation, and the change had been made by the tyrant's cunning to make him forget his family. Ellicott ends on the last clause, where the verb rendered troubles means literally to goad.
10:
The tree is taken for a common prophetic figure and then given a political meaning. Clarke observes that great men and princes are often represented under the similitude of trees, and lists the places; Ellicott names the same symbol of majesty and adds a parallel from a Greek historian, the dream of a Persian king. Calvin will not leave it at resemblance. Government exists, he says, for exactly this purpose, that rulers should be like trees on whose fruit all men feed and under whose shadow they rest, so that even tyrants, however far they have wandered from just and moderate rule, are trees whether they wish it or not, since it is better to live under the cruellest tyrant than under no government at all.

The growth of the tree is read as the growth of the empire. Gill takes each feature in turn: the tree growing higher and thicker is the increasing power and the stability of the dominion, the fair leaves are either the provinces or the governors under him, whose princes were altogether kings, and the abundance of fruit is what the empire yielded. Ellicott keeps to the picture, noting that it grew gradually larger in the vision, that the Greek version has the sun and moon dwelling in it and lighting the whole earth, and that the tree could be seen from the most distant parts of the known world. Calvin restricts the height deliberately, since there were other empires then but powerless or slight, and no prince could approach the Chaldean majesty, which makes a tree reaching to heaven unsurprising. He then dismisses two learned fancies in the same breath, that Babylon stood at the middle of the earth because it shared a parallel with Jerusalem, and that Jerusalem stood there instead, calling the first foolish and the second childish though ancient authors held it.

The watcher divides the readers by how much mythology they allow into it. Clarke reports that a watcher and a holy one are both angels, but of different orders according to the Chaldean oracles, a kind of judges of human actions with power to determine men's lot. Wesley keeps it simple, a holy angel, the instrument of God, the angels watching constantly to perform his judgments. Calvin argues the title from their nature: they are called watchers because they are perpetually awake in performing God's commands, not subject to slumber, not nourished by food or drink, and having no bodies at all, so that sleep, which follows from eating and drinking, has no place in them. Ellicott takes the boldest line, that the king dreamed in a language and out of an education familiar to him, so that by his own mythology he may have thought he saw one of his gods descending; and he points out that the prophet quietly corrects him, substituting the Most High where the king had said the watchers, and so assuring him that the decree is the one true God's and the watcher his angel.

The felling itself is described in short strokes. Gill says the angel cried with strengths, being mighty, so as to be heard far and near; Ellicott that he cried like a king's herald, and that the command to hew is plural, implying several employed to carry it out. Clarke reads the flight of the beasts as the desertion of the courtiers and officers, who abandoned the king as soon as his madness appeared, though he soon fled from human society himself. Calvin explains what taking away the heart means, and defends the roughness of it: a tree cannot properly be deprived of a human heart since it never had one, but the prophet bends a little aside from the strictness of the allegory because God mingled into the dream something by which the king might catch the meaning veiled under the image.
15:
The stump left standing is read by all as a mercy inside the sentence. Gill has the man not destroyed but continuing in a forlorn condition with hope of restoration, since a tree cut to the stump may revive; Clarke puts it in a line, that he is not to be destroyed nor his kingdom alienated. Ellicott adds the botany: just so much was left as could throw up a new sapling, and while the stump stood green branches might be hoped for. Calvin makes it the specimen of clemency in the punishment: hard as it is to be driven from human society and made like a wild beast, it is something in the man's favour that God does not tear him up by the roots but leaves what can be planted again.

The band about the stump is where the figure begins to break down. Ellicott says the typical language is gradually laid aside and a man begins to appear; the band is not a confined king's chains but trouble and affliction in the ordinary metaphorical sense. He argues against the assumption that the king wandered at large during his malady, calling it highly improbable, and reasons from the loyalty of courtiers who never used the sickness to set another man on the throne that he was confined in some court of his palace. By the next verse the metaphor is dropped altogether and a man spoken of outright.

The seven times are left deliberately undecided by one reader and settled by another. Clarke says the king was to continue in that state for seven years, and adds a case of his own acquaintance, a man who believed himself a bear and imitated the growl, in whom the thing did not appear hypochondriacal. Ellicott refuses the inference: the period meant by a time is very uncertain, the appeal to another passage for years purely conjectural, and it is likelier that some definite period was meant which the words over him suggest was marked by the heavenly bodies. Gill glosses the changed heart as changed not in substance but in quality.

The decree of the watchers raises the question of what angels have to do with it. Gill denies they are its authors and makes them approvers, ready to subscribe the sentence and to execute it against an oppressor of the Lord's people; he calls them assessors taken into consultation, on the analogy of a privy council, while allowing that nothing of the sort properly belongs to God. Wesley divides it the same way, the decree God's and the demand the angels', who consent to a just judgment put into their hands. Ellicott sharpens the division, assigning the request to the holy one and the execution to the watcher, and quotes a modern writer for the thought that this gives a glimpse into the angels' interest in ourselves: they longed that oppression should cease and prayed for the chastisement that would relieve the oppressed and convert the oppressor.

The clause about the Most High ruling carries the chapter's argument. Clarke insists that God never leaves the government of the world to men, to second causes or to chance, which are agents and not moving causes, and that the throne ennobles nobody, the king himself being given in mercy or in wrath; he illustrates from two successive rulers of his country, one of whom nearly ruined it and the other restored it. Wesley makes the same point against the flatterers who had allowed the king to be a god on earth accountable to none. Calvin reads the verse as confirming the dream: the king must know the punishment whose image he had seen cannot be escaped, the thing having been determined before God and his angels; and he rejects as too forced the reading that makes the angels ask a question merely to prove the point to onlookers.
19:
The prophet's silence is not read as puzzlement by anyone. Gill says the difficulty was not in the dream, which was plain and easy to him, but in the shocking things he saw coming on the king, so that he sat like a man thunderstruck, dumb and silent. Clarke says the same, that he was not puzzled by any obscurity but felt the delicacy of the thing, both for the king and for the nation. Henry supplies two causes at once, amazement and terror at so great a judgment on so great a prince, so that his flesh trembled for fear of God, and confusion at finding himself under a necessity of carrying heavy tidings to a man from whom he had received so many favours. Ellicott corrects the measure, noting that the word rendered an hour is literally a moment.

The greeting he opens with is admired as diplomacy of the right kind. Ellicott calls it a delicate way of expressing his hopes for the best, as though he had said, may what the interpretation implies overtake thine enemies instead. Wesley admires the whole short preface as showing address and an excellent spirit. Calvin turns it into a rule for ministers, and makes it the hardest one to keep. Some men are always fulminating under a pretence of zeal, forgetting that they too are men, showing no benevolence but only bitterness, so that they carry no authority and their admonitions are merely hated; others are perfidious flatterers who gloss over the grossest iniquities, and they cite the prophets and apostles as though the fervour of that zeal had driven out all human feeling. The middle course between the two is what the prophet keeps here.

Why the prophet should grieve for such a king at all is a question Calvin raises and answers. Cruel tyrant as the man was, and one who had all but destroyed the church, Daniel lived under his rule and was bound to pray for him; the exiles had been expressly taught by another prophet to seek the prosperity of Babylon, because their own peace lay in it. Until the seventy years were out it was not lawful either to indulge hatred against the king or to call down God's wrath on him, whatever might be asked afterwards.

On the interpretation itself the comments turn from feeling to geography. Gill and Clarke both treat the verses as needing no comment, since the dream explains itself once the tree is identified. Keil and Delitzsch observe how the interpretation proceeds, repeating the substance of the dream here and there in abbreviated form in the same words before declaring its reference to the king. Ellicott notices exactly that abbreviation and finds it worth remarking, since in the earlier dream the interpretation had on the contrary expanded the details.

The height of the tree is then cashed out as an empire. Ellicott takes the verse to mean that the king had arrived at the zenith of his power, and measures it: Armenia and much of Asia Minor to the north, Syria and at one time Egypt to the west, the Persian Gulf to the south, the Medes and Elamites subject in the east, so that holding two seas he had the treasures of the known world at command. He then makes the connection that carries the chapter's moral, that in the first vision this man had been shown as the golden head of an image, and that his sin was to want the whole image gold and himself to be the image. Wesley reckons the same extent by its seas, naming the northern, western and southern waters, and glosses the reach to heaven as the height of a majesty God had given him, which is the point on which the whole reproof will turn.
23:
Two grammatical points carry more weight here than their size suggests. Ellicott observes that a single word in the repetition stands for the whole latter part of the dream's command, another instance of the abbreviation he had noticed; and on the sentence of driving he explains that a third person plural active verb with an impersonal subject regularly does duty for a second person singular passive, so the words mean thou shalt be driven. Gill reaches the same rendering by another road, rejecting the family and the nobles as the drivers, since the nobles afterwards go looking for him; it is God who drives him, perhaps by ministering angels, or by his own imagination, suffered to prevail so far that a man who judged himself a beast found it most agreeable to live with beasts.

The watchers reappear and Ellicott makes an inference from the plural. The command in the dream had been ascribed to one watcher, while the interpretation says they commanded; from which he concludes that they form a council in which one acts for all. Gill leaves it that the order came from the Most High whoever carried it.

The clause promising the kingdom is read as the mercy in the sentence made explicit. Ellicott renders it literally shall arise, meaning that no successor should be appointed during the king's life, and notes that a phrase must be supplied before it to make the sense run. Clarke fills in the history, that no new king was set up and the king's son acted as regent through his father's insanity. Ellicott glosses the reason given, that the heavens, or One in heaven, rule the kingdoms of men. Wesley marks the effect the speech should have had, calling it such a thundering peal that it is wonderful the king endured it without fury boiling in him, and observing how hard a lesson this is for lofty princes.

The counsel that follows turns on two words. Calvin notes that interpreters do not agree even about the first, since the word may be read my counsel or my king, both coming from the same root; he settles for counsel. On the second the three of them converge against a familiar rendering. Ellicott takes the metaphor from a refractory beast casting off the yoke, so that the prophet tells the king to rebel against his own sins of pride and cruelty and put them aside by practising the contrary virtues; he then states flatly that the Chaldee words carry neither the idea of alms nor of redeeming, so the translation redeem thy sins by alms is incorrect and unwarrantable. Calvin agrees that the verb often means to break or abolish and reads break off thy sins by pity and humanity, so that cruelty is changed into clemency. Clarke keeps the plain imperative, do justice, and applies it: the king had been an oppressive man and should show mercy to the poor whom he had himself made poor, the whole Jewish nation being witness.

The last clause is felt to be carefully guarded. Wesley admires that the prophet was neither certain of pardon for the king nor altogether despairing of it, and speaks with wisdom and tenderness and yet with plainness. Ellicott reads it as a straightforward condition, that if the king repents his prosperity and peace will be prolonged. Gill notices the delicacy of the approach itself, a minister and servant asking a king to take his advice in good part as offered from a hearty concern for his welfare. Calvin draws the doctrine he thinks depends on the reading: an end is to be made of sin and a new course entered, the tyrannical violence giving way to clemency, which is why the sense of the verb matters so much. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the structure of the address without adding to it.
28:
The change of person occupies the readers who notice it. Keil and Delitzsch record that some critics take the narrative tone as evidence that somebody other than the king framed the edict, and answer that the first person returns a few verses later, so the change has its reason in the matter itself; they also refuse the explanation that he found it unbecoming to speak of his madness in his own person, since a man so tender of himself would not have published the affair at all. Calvin treats it as ordinary usage among Hebrews and Chaldeans, and takes the prophet to be giving the substance of the king's words rather than the words themselves. Wesley admires the propriety of it, six verses in the third person and the first resumed as soon as reason returns.

The twelve months are read as a mercy, though not by everyone in the same way. Gill dates them and says the year was either given for repentance or gained by the king's attending a while to the advice. Ellicott says plainly that sufficient time for repentance was mercifully granted. Calvin will not have it. He thinks it improbable that the king was touched at all and the punishment therefore deferred; God withdrew his hand till the year ended, which made the pride less excusable, since a prophet's voice should have frightened the man as if God had thundered from heaven. He grants that God sometimes indulges the reprobate when he sees them humbled, citing a king spared without repenting cordially, but does not think that happened here.

The boast itself is set against the city it was made in. Ellicott gives the measurements: two hundred square miles, walls of enormous width and height with brazen gates on terraces facing the river, the interior laid out in smaller towns divided by parks and plantations, corn enough within the walls for the whole population, and eight temples the king had finished besides the great one across the river. Walking on the flat roof of that palace with all this before him, he says, the king spoke words that were true and yet showed what the twelve months had come to. Clarke says the same more briefly: the heart was inflated, he attributed everything to himself and acknowledged God in nothing. Ellicott adds that the palace was the one in Babylon itself, the king being at the centre of his dominions when it happened, so there is no need to suppose the account written by someone far away.

The interruption is heard as an echo. Ellicott notes that the voice would have reminded the king of the crying watcher in his dream, and Clarke marks the awfulness of the moment for a victorious king, all his goods and gods gone at once. Gill has the voice heard by the king and all about him, formed by angels, and cites a writer who reports that when the king had finished such an oration he immediately disappeared.

What the malady was is where the accounts differ most. Clarke describes the man forsaking society for woods and deserts, his hair growing thick enough to serve for clothing and his nails hooked for climbing and grubbing roots, and calls it God's mercy that he was so clothed. Ellicott names it, saying it is now generally agreed to have been the mania called lycanthropy, and observes that the sufferer kept his consciousness, since he lifts up his eyes before his understanding returns; the histories say nothing of the illness, though the king's own inscriptions show an interval in which no great public works were executed. Gill is concerned to deny any real change of nature, since a man turned into a beast would not be the same person and so not the one punished; the alteration touched body and mind severely while the essential parts of a man remained.
34:
The lifting of the eyes is treated as the first act of a returning man. Henry sets the picture: he looked no longer down towards the earth as a beast but began to look up as a man, and quotes the old line that heaven gave to man an erect countenance; but he insists more is meant, since the man looks up as a penitent making a humble petition, perhaps only now made sensible of his misery. He adds the reckoning that goes with it, that those may justly be counted void of understanding who do not bless God, and that men never rightly use their reason until they begin to be religious. Wesley says the same in a sentence, that God shone on his soul and gave him understanding to consider his sad state and its causes. Ellicott corrects the psychology: by his understanding is meant not consciousness so much as his sense of personality, which had been lost for a time.

Calvin takes the delay itself as the lesson. That it was seven years before the man began to raise his eyes shows how long it takes to cure pride, since a vital part once corrupt is slow and difficult to heal, and pride that has got into the marrow and infected the inmost soul is not easily plucked out. He draws from this that God's word may operate on a man without the effect of grace appearing at once. Gill dates the recovery precisely and adds that the king lived a single year afterwards, reigning forty-three from his father's death, or forty-five by the Jewish reckoning, which counts from his partnership in the kingdom.

The doxology raises a question about who wrote the letter. Ellicott observes that the words about the everlasting dominion, like those near the beginning, recall a psalm, and that the verse following is not unlike several places in another prophet; and he thinks it hard to suppose the king so thoroughly versed in the Hebrew scriptures as to be able to use them for doxologies. This, he says, supports the conjecture that the letter was composed by Daniel rather than by the king himself.

The clause about the inhabitants of the earth being nothing is carefully qualified rather than simply repeated. Gill will not let it stand absolutely: taken in themselves men are something, their bodies remarkable in their origin and make and even in their dissolution, and their souls more valuable still, being immaterial and immortal and worth more than the whole world; it is only comparatively, with respect to the God in whom they live and move, that they are as nothing. Wesley reaches the same qualification from the other end, listing the senses in which the creature is nothing: nothing to help, nothing to hurt, nothing in duration, nothing solid, nothing without dependence and support from God. Calvin makes the contrast the whole point of the sentence, since the eternity of God is confessed in words by everyone while few descend into themselves to weigh their own frailty, and men unmindful of their own lot rage against God. He also weighs the disputed word, reporting the reading that takes it as a noun meaning anything, from a root meaning to finish or consume, so that men are limited within their own standard while God is immense; he calls that harsh and prefers the received view, that one letter here stands for another and the sense is that men are esteemed of no value before him.

Keil and Delitzsch look ahead from the verse to what it produces, marking the inward connection between the return of reason and the restoration of the throne, which is why the first element is repeated before the second follows in the plain manner of Semitic narrative.
36:
The restoration of the kingdom is a wonder in its own right. Clarke notes that everything the dream exhibited was fulfilled, and adds that the king's hiding place had probably never been found, so that on his return his counsellors and lords received him gladly and served him as before. Wesley describes what returned with the reason: the majesty of a king in his countenance, the wonted power and place, owned and obeyed by all, and a prince more august than before. Ellicott glosses the phrase about glory as the splendour returning so as to increase the honour of the reign. Gill notes that the repetition marks both the certainty of it and the man's sense of how great the favour was.

Calvin makes the restoration a second creation. The man was never turned into a brute, but was treated with such ignominy, made like the wild beasts and pastured with them, that God's forming a man again out of a beast may be called a kind of new creation. That is why the thanksgiving dwells on understanding and reason, which he calls inestimable blessings, and why the king says it twice: he had experienced a singular grace in being returned to a sound mind, and commends a mercy content with a temporary chastisement.

The closing doxology is read as confession as much as praise. Gill has the king now knowing that the heavens rule and that there is a God above all gods and kings, who brought him low and raised him up; and he gives his praise in the most public way, by word before his lords and by writing under his own hand. Calvin hears a confession of fault inside the thanksgiving: what is said about the proud the king applies to himself, as though God had made him a monument of his method of humbling the proud, for the instruction of mankind, since his haughtiness could not have been arrested by a lighter remedy. Keil and Delitzsch render the two attributes truth and judgment, and agree that the king recognised his humiliation as a righteous punishment for pride.

Whether the man was actually converted is the chapter's last and sharpest dispute. Keil and Delitzsch put the negative case, that he says nothing of the grace shown him, and report the conclusion drawn from this that he was never brought to true heart-repentance. Clarke takes the opposite view, thinking it very probable he was a true convert who relapsed no more and died in the faith of the God of Israel. Wesley challenges the other side directly, asking what authority anyone had to say this man was no convert, and declaring that we can no more doubt his salvation than Solomon's; the doxology proceeds from the heart, the king acknowledging that God dealt justly with him for his pride, afflicted him in faithfulness and restored him in tenderness, so that he has no ground to quarrel but only to give glory by confession.

Ellicott declines to settle it and traces a progress. At the first interview the king's belief rose no higher than a heathen's in his own superstitions; it grew into a confession that this God was a revealer of secrets, though still not equal to his own; the furnace showed how little depth that had, since he set himself above all gods, and afterwards he owned the Most High while keeping him level with his own chief deity. Here he recognises that same Most High as the cause of his recovery and praises the King of heaven. Holding the Babylonian theory of sickness, he must have supposed himself under an evil spirit and been treated by his magicians with charms and amulets and images of his gods; the thanksgiving makes it possible to suppose he had let much of that go and was advancing towards the truth, if not already in possession of it.
